articles.title: How to Identify the gcware Leader Node in a GBase 8a Cluster
articles.excerpt: In GBase 8a, the China-domestically developed MPP analytical database from GBASE, the gcware service cluster shares information between the GCluster instances on every node — cluster topology, node st…
articles.body: In GBase 8a, the China-domestically developed MPP analytical database from GBASE, the gcware service cluster shares information between the GCluster instances on every node — cluster topology, node states, node resource states — and, during multi-replica data operations, decides which nodes are usable and controls data-consistency state. A gcware cluster has several nodes, usually an odd number : one is elected leader , the rest are followers , and the leader holds the most current data. This post shows how to find out which node that is.

articles.title: Spring Data JPA Explained: JpaRepository, JPQL, Transactions and ResponseEntity
articles.excerpt: In Part 1, we learned how Spring manages objects using @Component, @Service, and @Repository. In Part 2, we learned how Java communicates with databases using JDBC and how Spring simplifies database o…
articles.body: In Part 1, we learned how Spring manages objects using @Component , @Service , and @Repository . In Part 2, we learned how Java communicates with databases using JDBC and how Spring simplifies database operations using JdbcTemplate . But there is another question. Do we really need to write SQL queries for every database operation? Imagine Asha is building a library management application. She wants to perform operations like: Save a new book. Find a book by its ID. Fetch all books. Update book information. Delete a book. With JDBC, we write SQL queries and map the returned rows into Java objects. It works perfectly, but writing SQL and mapping database records manually for every operation can become repetitive. Wouldn't it be nice if we could work directly with Java objects instead?

articles.title: How Much Can I Spend Per Day? A Salary Formula for India
articles.excerpt: Quick answer: Your daily spending limit is (take-home salary − fixed costs − savings) ÷ days left until your next salary, counting today. On a ₹45,000 salary with ₹18,000 of rent, EMI and bills and ₹6…
articles.body: Quick answer: Your daily spending limit is (take-home salary − fixed costs − savings) ÷ days left until your next salary, counting today. On a ₹45,000 salary with ₹18,000 of rent, EMI and bills and ₹6,000 saved, that is ₹21,000 ÷ 30 = ₹700 a day . Most budgets ask you to plan 10 or 12 categories at the start of the month and then never look at them again. A daily number works differently. You get one figure each morning, and if you stay under it, the month works out. This guide shows how to get that figure for your own salary, with the arithmetic written out so you can check it. If you'd rather not do the sums by hand, the daily budget calculator does the same maths. The formula, in plain words There are three steps. Find the money you can actually spend.

articles.title: 27,197 Product URLs Across 14 Sitemap Shards: What Splitting Bought Us
articles.excerpt: Our sitemap index used to be one file with a single product sitemap under it. That sitemap listed 27,197 URLs in one XML document. It was 6.8 MB uncompressed. Search Console did not complain. It repor…
articles.body: Our sitemap index used to be one file with a single product sitemap under it. That sitemap listed 27,197 URLs in one XML document. It was 6.8 MB uncompressed. Search Console did not complain. It reported the sitemap as "Success." That is the trap: a green tick in Search Console means the file parsed, not that Google crawled a useful share of it. The signal that made us look Crawl stats showed 4,100–5,200 product URLs fetched per day against 27,197 total. At that rate a full pass takes five to six days. That is acceptable. What was not acceptable was the distribution: the newest 2,000 products were being fetched repeatedly while pages published four months earlier had not been touched in three weeks.
articles.author: Visen

articles.title: The Search Box Was Fine. The Synonym Table Was Empty.
articles.excerpt: A customer typed rlx submariner into our search field and got "No results found." The product was in the catalog. The title contained "Submariner." The search box worked exactly as written. The proble…
articles.body: A customer typed rlx submariner into our search field and got "No results found." The product was in the catalog. The title contained "Submariner." The search box worked exactly as written. The problem was that nothing in our stack knew rlx meant Rolex . We only found it because we sampled twenty real searches from our site search log and ran each one twice — once with the exact product title, once with the shortened form people actually type. Nine of the twenty returned different result sets. Four returned nothing at all. Why store search fails on abbreviations WooCommerce search runs a LIKE against post title and content. It does not stem, it does not expand, and it has no concept of a brand alias. If the abbreviation is not literally in the title, the query misses.

articles.body: When I started learning Spring Boot, I kept seeing annotations like @Component , @Service , and @Repository everywhere. Initially, I thought they were just different ways of telling Spring to create objects. But then I started wondering: Why do we need three different annotations? What exactly is a Spring Bean? articles.body: The December full moon reaches peak illumination at 8:28 p.m. EST on Dec. 23 (0128 GMT on Dec. 24) as the lunar disk shines opposite the sun in Earth's sky. It is often called the "Cold Moon" in reference to the frigid temperatures that prevail in the Northern Hemisphere around the time of its rising, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac . December's full moon will also occur close to perigee — the moon's closest point to Earth in its elliptical orbit — giving rise to a spectacular supermoon. A supermoon can appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than a full moon at its farthest point from Earth (also known as a micromoon)..

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 25, 1970: NASA's 'wingless' M2-F3 'lifting body' aircraft makes its 1st powered flight ahead of supersonic tests
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight. The M2-F3 aircraft was a heavyweight "lifting body" designed to test its ability to produce most of its lift through its fuselage instead of wings. It's commonly referred to as a "wingless" aircraft. After Air Force test pilot Bill Dana took the M2-F3 on three unpowered glide test flights, he did the first powered flight, too. Dana soared to an altitude of 45,000 feet during this flight, which lasted just over 6 minutes. He didn't break the sound barrier this time, but he did on later flights. The M2-F3 flew a total of 27 missions in its three-year flight history. Its top speed was 1.6 times the speed of sound, and its top altitude was 71,500 feet.
